In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed methods for estimating prediction error in survival models provide a useful tool for assessing the performance of statistical models in practice, and can help to guide model selection and to assess the accuracy of model predictions.

cross‐validation is the preferred method for estimating the prediction error for survival analysis models, especially in the presence of variable selection or misspecified models, and when the goal is to estimate prediction error for point predictors.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cross-validation method is the most reliable method to estimate the prediction error, and that the model-based method is sensitive to model miss-specification.

we are able to provide a reliable point estimate and confidence interval for prediction error for a variety of loss functions, even in the presence of model misspecification, by applying a simple cross‐validation procedure.
cross-validation procedures typically produce reliable estimates for point prediction, whereas model-based estimates can be sensitive to model misspecificaion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cross‐validation is a robust procedure for estimating prediction error in a survival context.
cross‐validation methods can be used to produce accurate point and interval estimates of prediction error.
cross‐validation methods are reliable in the sense that they produce point estimates and confidence limits that are close to the true values.
